Prayer of Faith
PRAIR uv FAITH
noun phrase
From Old English præger (prayer, petition) and Old English geleafa (belief, trust, from Germanic galaubijan, to believe). The phrase renders the Greek euchē tēs pisteōs (the prayer of faith, Jas. 5:15), a construction tying faithful petition to the covenant promises of the God who hears. The phrase has been consistently misread by the Word of Faith movement as a guarantee of healing-on-demand, but its meaning in James is covenantal confidence in the will of God rather than psychological certainty about a desired outcome.

Biblical Definition

The prayer of faith is the confident petition offered to God in trust of His covenant promises and in submission to His sovereign will — the mode of prayer that characterizes the righteous man whose “effective prayer” can “accomplish much” (Jas. 5:16). James commands the elders to pray over the sick, anointing with oil in the Lord's name, and promises that “the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick — and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him” (Jas. 5:15). The immediate context is the church's pastoral ministry to the suffering, not a general formula for obtaining any desired outcome.

The prayer of faith is not a technique for bending God's will to human desire. Christ Himself modeled the prayer of faith in Gethsemane: “And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” (Matt. 26:39) — a perfect prayer of faith precisely because it entrusted the Father with the outcome. First John 5:14 defines the scope: “This is the confidence that we have toward Him: that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.” Confidence is warranted; coercion of the divine will is not. Philippians 4:6 adds the shape: “by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” — a pattern of surrender, not seizure. The prayer of faith is therefore the prayer that trusts God enough to submit the petition to His wisdom and His timing, confident that He who did not spare His own Son will with Him freely give all things (Rom. 8:32).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined faith as “belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity.” The prayer of faith is petition offered from this posture — trusting the character and promise of the One addressed rather than demanding a specific outcome.

FAITH, n. [L. fides; It. fede; Fr. foi.] Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity, without other evidence.

In theology, the assent of the mind or understanding to the truth of what God has revealed. Faith is an assent to the truth of the scriptures, or rather the cordial reception of the gospel salvation; the belief of the great doctrines of the gospel, and a firm reliance on the merits and righteousness of Christ for pardon, acceptance, and salvation.

PRAYER, n. In theology, a solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, confession, supplication, and thanksgiving. Prayer is distinguished from petition in that it includes reverence, confession, and praise in addition to asking.

The prayer of faith (Jas. 5:15): the confident, believing petition offered to God in trust of His covenant promise and in submission to His sovereign will — distinguished from presumptuous demand, from faithless anxiety, and from the mechanical recitation of words without genuine confidence in the God addressed.

Word of Faith distortion: the teaching of Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland, and associated teachers that the prayer of faith is a spiritual law by which believers “claim” healing, prosperity, and desired outcomes — treating faith as a force rather than a relational posture of confidence in the Person and promises of God.

Key Scripture

James 5:15 — "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him."

1 John 5:14 — "And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:"

Matt. 21:22 — "And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive."

Phil. 4:6 — "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."

Modern Corruption

The Word of Faith movement has turned the prayer of faith into a spiritual technique by which believers compel God to produce desired outcomes, substituting psychological confidence for covenantal trust and naming-and-claiming for submission to God's sovereign will.

expand to see more

The primary corruption of the prayer of faith is the Word of Faith theology of Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland, Benny Hinn, and their successors, who teach that faith is a spiritual “force” and that words spoken in faith release that force to produce the desired reality. On this account, the prayer of faith is a technique: visualize the outcome, speak it with sufficient confidence, do not waver, and the spiritual laws will produce it. This is not biblical faith; it is a Christian-sounding form of New Thought occultism, which teaches that the mind's positive confession can shape material reality. The prayer of faith in James 5 is offered by the church elders over the sick in submission to the Lord who “raises him up” — the initiative, the power, and the decision belong to God, not to the quality of the petitioner's faith-confession.

A second corruption of the prayer of faith operates at the opposite extreme: a faithless, rote petitioning that has no actual expectation of being heard, offered as a religious duty without genuine confidence in the covenant God. The corruption here is not presumption but unbelief — prayer as an anxiety management practice rather than genuine address to the living God who hears and answers. The reforming word is the promise of Matthew 21:22 and 1 John 5:14 taken together: all things asked in faith are received, but faith is asking according to God's will, confident in His goodness and wisdom, not demanding a specific outcome. The prayer of faith is the prayer of a child who trusts his Father completely — and therefore does not need to dictate the terms of the answer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase prayer of faith binds together the act of petition with the posture of trust, establishing that genuine prayer is not the mere voicing of requests but the covenantal address of a trusting creature to a faithful God.

expand to see more

Greek euchē (εὐχή) — a wish, a prayer, a vow; used in James 5:15 in the compound euchē tēs pisteōs (the prayer of faith); distinct from proseuche (habitual, devoted prayer) and deēsis (urgent petition); the word carries the sense of a specific, directed request

Greek pistis (πίστισ) — faith, trust, confidence; the noun from which pisteōs (genitive, “of faith”) derives; in James 5:15 it modifies the prayer — the prayer that proceeds from and is characterized by genuine covenantal trust in God

Latin fides (faith, trust, loyalty) — the Vulgate renders pistis as fides; entering English through Old French as faith; the word carries the personal relational sense of loyalty and trust between persons, not merely intellectual assent

James 5:13–18 context: James grounds the prayer of faith in the concrete pastoral practice of the church (elders anointing the sick) and in the biblical precedent of Elijah, whose prayer “was heard” (Jas. 5:17–18) — establishing that the effectual prayer is the prayer of a righteous man, not the prayer of the most psychologically confident

Reformation commentary: Calvin on James 5:15 insisted that the prayer of faith does not guarantee physical healing in every case but that the elders' prayer, offered in faith, entrusts the sick person to God's will — which may include healing, or may include bearing the affliction for spiritual profit, or may include faithful death

Usage

"The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 178–185) describes the proper manner of prayer as including “with faith, reverence, humility, fervency, love, and perseverance” — a description that captures the prayer of faith without reducing it to a psychological technique or a spiritual formula."

"John Calvin in the Institutes (III.20) devoted extensive treatment to prayer, insisting that faith is not the source of prayer's efficacy — God's covenant promise is the source — but faith is the hand that grasps the promise; the prayer of faith is the prayer that clings to what God has pledged rather than demanding what God has not promised."

"The faithful elder who prays over the dying saint, anointing with oil in the Lord's name (Jas. 5:14), performs the prayer of faith not when he guarantees a specific outcome but when he commits the sufferer fully to the God who raises up — and who raised up His own Son from the dead, guaranteeing that no believer's suffering is the final word."
